title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: 87% identify line manager effectiveness as a significant risk while 21% provide toolkits `[V]`. What kind of gap is that?
options: A competence gap — communicators don't know how to build manager materials
A stated-priority-versus-investment gap, which almost always means the intervention was unaffordable rather than unwanted
A measurement gap — organizations don't track manager effectiveness accurately
An awareness gap — most organizations don't realize managers matter
questions.explanation: The same respondents naming the risk are the ones without the resources to close it. That reading matters because it determines the argument you make: you're pointing at a named top risk that was never resourced, and explaining that the reason has gone away.

questions.prompt: What do managers actually need that a generic talking-points document can't provide?
options: Shorter documents with clearer formatting
Earlier access to the message before it goes to employees
The local version — their team's specific exposure, the questions their people will actually ask, what will land badly here, and language that passes the read-aloud test
Training in how to deliver difficult messages
questions.explanation: The document was written for the average manager, and no manager is average. D is a real need and it is the counter-argument, not this lesson.

questions.prompt: Why was personalized manager enablement impossible before, in precise terms?
options: The data to segment on didn't exist
Because 40 minutes per manager × 400 managers is roughly 260 person-days per significant change — arithmetic, not budget
Because managers wouldn't have used it
Because legal review couldn't scale to that many variants
questions.explanation: Which is why every organization ships the generic version and calls the gap a budget problem. Now the 40 minutes of thinking happens once, centrally, and generation is close to free.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes sharing data *with* a manager from sharing it *about* them?
options: Whether the data is quantitative or qualitative
Whether it is shared before or after a review cycle
*About* arrives as assessment, so the rational response is to manage the number; *with* arrives as usable intelligence that makes them better at a job they're already trying to do
Whether the manager's own team can see it
questions.explanation: Their engagement score against the company average is a grade. "Here's what your team asked about most, and the three things they searched for and didn't find" is material. Same underlying data, opposite effect.

questions.prompt: What must be true for *with* not to collapse back into *about*?
options: It must be delivered by the manager's own leader
It must not be comparative by default, and it must run inside the listening charter — if the charter and this module's ambition conflict, the charter wins
It must be anonymized before the manager sees it
It must be optional for the manager to receive
questions.explanation: The moment a manager's number sits next to their peers', it is assessment regardless of framing. And a manager-enablement programme that quietly breaches a listening promise destroys the listening programme, which is the more valuable asset.

questions.prompt: Why does AI making local variation free create a problem for cascades?
options: Because managers lack the skill to adapt messages well
Because each individual version is often better, and in aggregate you get four hundred slightly different accounts of a restructure — which is how an organization acquires commitments it never made
Because localized messages take longer to review
Because employees prefer to receive the official version
questions.explanation: Consistency was the entire purpose of a cascade. The response isn't to forbid improvisation — it's to build the distinction into the kit so managers improvise in the right places.

questions.prompt: Which category does "the date the change takes effect, and which roles are affected" belong to?
options: Should vary locally — the manager knows how to frame it for their team
Shouldn't be in the kit — it requires judgment the manager isn't equipped to make
Must stay identical — it's a commitment that will be compared across teams, and a rephrasing reads as incompetence or concealment
It depends on whether the manager's team is directly affected
questions.explanation: And the kit should say *why* it's fixed. Managers comply with constraints they understand and route around ones they don't.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest argument *against* this module's claim?
options: That manager toolkits have never been shown to improve message retention

That the constraint was never production cost — managers avoid these conversations because delivering bad news is hard, they often disagree with the decision, and they're protecting long-term relationships. A better kit touches none of that
That personalization at scale creates unacceptable data-protection exposure
That managers prefer to receive less material, not more
questions.explanation: And it has a sharper edge for this audience: personalized kits may make it *worse*, by making it easier to deliver a message you don't believe without the friction that used to force you to work out what you thought. Which is why the activity asks what you actually saw in a real manager.
